title: From reactive relief to zero-casualty resolve: How Naya Bharat built a world-class disaster shield since 2014
excerpt: Since 2014, under the decisive leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Bharat has transformed its disaster management from a slow, reactive relief model into a proactive, zero-casualty mission. By tripling disaster response funds to around Rs2 lakh crore, launching dedicated mitigation funds, and empowering grassroots ‘Aapada Mitra’ volunteers alongside advanced weather forecasting, the government has built a self-reliant and resilient Naya Bharat. Through landmark initiatives like the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) and swift global rescue missions such as Operation Dost, Bharat has not only secured its own citizens against natural calamities but has also emerged as a trusted Vishwaguru and global leader in humanitarian assistance. On October 28, 2026, when Cyclone Arnab made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh–Yanam coast, Bharat’s strengthened disaster management framework effectively protected lives and property. According to official assessments of the response, accurate early weather forecasting, proactive mass evacuations, seamless coordination across government agencies, and the swift deployment of NDRF and SDRF personnel kept casualties and infrastructure damage to a minimum. The operation highlighted the country’s modern, self-reliant approach to handling severe natural calamities and safeguarding its citizens. This report highlights how Bharat has modernised its disaster management system since 2014 through policy reforms, resilient infrastructure, advanced technology, increased funding, and faster emergency responses to protect lives and property. Proactive Policy Approach: Bharat moved away from reactive relief toward advance preparedness through the 2016 National Disaster Management Plan (aligned with the UN Sendai Framework) and the Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda. Grassroots Volunteer Network: The Aapda Mitra scheme grew from 5,186 volunteers in 30 districts to a target of 1 lakh trained and insured community responders across 350 multi-hazard districts, alongside the Yuva Aapda Mitra initiative engaging NCC, NSS, and Bharat Scouts and Guides. Resilient Infrastructure: Bharat built cyclone shelters, evacuation roads, bridges, underground power cables, river embankments, Himalayan slope stabilization, and rockfall barriers to withstand severe weather events. Advanced Early-Warning Systems: Upgrades in weather tracking using Doppler radars, tsunami monitoring, storm-surge modelling, satellite drought assessments, and the Damini lightning-alert app, supported by the Rs 2,000 crore Mission Mausam for AI-based forecasting. Increased Funding and Rapid Action: For the 2021–26 period, allocations of Rs1.60 lakh crore for SDRF and SDMF, Rs54,770 crore for NDRF, and Rs13,693 crore for NDMF, while Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT) deployment times dropped from 96 days to 8 days by 2025. Transforming Bharat’s Disaster Governance: A Shift Toward Proactive Resilience Since 2014, Bharat has fundamentally transformed its disaster governance framework, moving away from a reactive, post-disaster relief model toward a decisive, proactive strategy centred on early warnings, risk reduction, and minimising the loss of lives and property. Overcoming Past Fragmentation: Prior to 2014, despite the enactment of the Disaster Management Act of 2005, Bharat’s disaster response remained largely fragmented and reactive. Authorities often struggled with poor co-ordination, staffing shortages, and the lack of a unified operational strategy, which led to delayed responses during major crises. The Landmark National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP): A decisive turning point occurred in May 2016 with the launch of Bharat’s first comprehensive National Disaster Management Plan. Later updated in November 2019 to address climate change and localised risks, the NDMP established a clear, unified roadmap for the entire nation. Global Standards and “Build Back Better”: The NDMP aligned Bharat’s strategy with the four core priorities of the United Nations Sendai Framework (2015–2030): understanding disaster risks, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and enhancing response preparedness. It also embedded the principle of “Build Back Better” into recovery and reconstruction efforts. The Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda: Announced at the Asian Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in New Delhi in November 2016, the Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda turned these broad goals into concrete action. Inclusive and Technology-Driven Development: This agenda mandated that all development sectors integrate disaster risk management into their projects. It placed a strong emphasis on safeguarding vulnerable households and small businesses, empowering women to take leadership roles in disaster management, and investing heavily in multi-hazard mapping, modern technology, and stronger institutions. Empowering Citizens on the Frontlines: Building a Self-Reliant Disaster Response Under the Modi government’s vision of Jan Bhagidari (people’s participation), Bharat has transformed disaster response from a purely government-led effort into a nationwide grassroots movement. By training ordinary citizens and youth as first responders, the nation is building a resilient, self-reliant society capable of protecting communities before formal relief forces even arrive. Massive Expansion of Aapda Mitra: Spearheaded by the Central Government through the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), the Aapda Mitra scheme trains local residents to act as immediate first responders. After a successful pilot between 2016 and 2018 that trained 5,186 volunteers across 30 flood-prone districts, the initiative was scaled up nationwide to certify and equip 1,00,000 community volunteers across 350 multi-hazard districts in every state and Union Territory. Hands-On Training by Elite Forces: Volunteers undergo an intensive five-day training program led by master trainers from the NDRF and SDRF. They learn life-saving skills including CPR, first aid, flood rescue, basic search and rescue, navigating collapsed structures, and safely evacuating vulnerable citizens. Comprehensive Gear and Insurance Protection: To ensure these grassroots heroes are well-protected, every trained volunteer receives an Emergency Responder Kit equipped with a safety helmet, life jacket, protective gear, LED torch, first-aid supplies, multi-tool knife, and emergency whistle. Additionally, the government provides each enrolled volunteer with three years of life and disability insurance coverage. Proven Impact on the Ground: Aapda Mitra volunteers have already proven their worth during major crises, including Cyclone Fani in Odisha, the Kerala floods, and the Wayanad landslide. Working shoulder-to-shoulder with local authorities, they played a crucial role in delivering early warnings, guiding evacuations, administering first aid, and distributing essential relief materials. Mobilising Bharat’s Youth with Yuva Aapda Mitra: Recognising the energy and discipline of Bharat’s youth, the government launched the Yuva Aapda Mitra initiative. This programme partners with premier youth organisations-the NCC, NSS, and Bharat Scouts and Guides-to build a dedicated cadre of young, disaster-ready citizens across the country. title: AI and digital disruptions in the US: Real manthan for “Artificial” disturbance
excerpt: Those in the digital technology world will know that a series of seemingly unrelated events occurred within six days, raising national security questions in the United States of America. First, on Thursday, November 12, Microsoft’s services went down worldwide. Outlook email, Teams and Copilot failed in more than 70 countries, and it took almost two days to fully restore them for the roughly 43 crore (430 million) people who use Microsoft 365. Bharat was not spared: employees at Infosys and Cognizant, Tata Motors, and airlines such as IndiGo and Air India all reported disruptions. On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which controls American airspace, ordered a nationwide “ground stop”, meaning no aircraft anywhere in the US was allowed to take off. It lasted more than four hours, and about 3,500 planes were in the air when the order was given. Such a grounding has happened only three times in history: after the terror attacks of September 11, 2001, during a computer failure in January 2023, and now. On Monday, issues hit JP Morgan Chase, America’s largest bank, and United Airlines, one of its largest airlines. Then, on Tuesday, a classified internal communications network of the National Security Agency (NSA), America’s electronic intelligence agency, slowed down, while other large corporations like Apple and Marriott also experienced issues. Bank of America, another major bank, also reported disruptions during the same period. Each organisation has given its own explanation: a wrong network setting at Microsoft, new equipment installed during an upgrade at an FAA facility in Arkansas, a software bug at Chase, routine maintenance at the NSA, and an internal update at Apple. American officials, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, insist there is “zero evidence” linking these events to each other or to a foreign hand. Still, so many failures in so few days are so unusual that they cannot be taken as one-offs. In addition, these digital disruptions have affected and disrupted national life in the US, and every pundit has jumped in to analyse what happened. Suspicions range from foreign sabotage to rogue Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents and conspiracies. The suspicion ran so deep that Microsoft had to state publicly that its outage was “not related to cyber or AI/agents”. Digital Disruptions, Deeper Questions Those who heeded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s call for Swadeshi about a year ago saw the benefits of Digital Sovereignty. After that call, Union Ministers like Ashwini Vaishnaw and Amit Shah publicly moved to Zoho, the homegrown software company from Tamil Nadu, and the National Informatics Centre has since migrated about 12.7 lakh government email accounts to a Zoho-based platform. Their systems didn’t go down with Microsoft’s; switching to Zoho helped them avoid the issues. No wonder Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw of Biocon called the outage “an unexpected opportunity” for Zoho to become the backup for India Inc. However, some would argue that Microsoft’s systems went down or slowed down as the price of the largest security clean-up in its history. Using AI, Microsoft found and fixed more than 1,400 historic security vulnerabilities in October alone and almost 1,100 more on November 10, just two days before the outage. A year ago, the normal figure was about 100 a month. Microsoft itself blames a network setting, not these fixes, but the argument is that a company changing its systems at this pace will stumble at times, and that this is a small price to pay for the more robust systems being implemented. Those whose systems were never probed by AI for security vulnerabilities can claim they are safer. Still, they are not, because those that don’t upgrade or use AI daily will fall behind in the ever-evolving digital space. Some argue that most recent system outages in America stem from AI-supported upgrades that companies are implementing rapidly to stay ahead of a new breed of hackers from outside America. Even America’s Director of National Intelligence has blamed the patching and upgrading of systems, not an enemy. America claims it is about six months ahead of competitors like China in evolving AI. On the same Thursday that Microsoft went down, Jensen Huang, who led Nvidia for 33 years, resigned as CEO under pressure from its board. Nvidia makes about 90 per cent of the advanced chips that run AI and was, until recently, the world’s most valuable company, worth more than five trillion dollars at its peak. He left amidst reports of a personal relationship with a woman whom American intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China. Nothing has been proven against him, and Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe national security was compromised. Yet a frenzy has built up in America over the belief that China is out to get America. I believe the real story is not about America or China. It is really about our lives and the lives of future generations of humans and their freedoms. What AI Really Is? Humanity is at a juncture where, in pursuing productivity, we have discovered that all the data, information and knowledge stored in books and other digital formats since human civilisation began can be self-organised with a small nudge from simple algorithms that have been known for the last four to five decades. The method used to train today’s AI, called backpropagation, was popularised as far back as 1986. The only missing ingredient was the capacity and speed to iteratively group related information into bundles based on the context in which that knowledge is needed. This is now happening, and we call it Artificial Intelligence. The main driving force behind this self-reorganisation of information is advancement in computing speed and capacity, which we refer to as semiconductor chips. That is why a chip company like Nvidia became the most valuable company in the world, and why the fall of its CEO is treated in America as a national security matter. title: From reactive relief to zero-casualty resolve: How Naya Bharat built a world-class disaster shield since 2014
excerpt: Since 2014, under the decisive leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Bharat has transformed its disaster management from a slow, reactive relief model into a proactive, zero-casualty mission. By tripling disaster response funds to around Rs2 lakh crore, launching dedicated mitigation funds, and empowering grassroots ‘Aapada Mitra’ volunteers alongside advanced weather forecasting, the government has built a self-reliant and resilient Naya Bharat. Through landmark initiatives like the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) and swift global rescue missions such as Operation Dost, Bharat has not only secured its own citizens against natural calamities but has also emerged as a trusted Vishwaguru and global leader in humanitarian assistance. On October 28, 2026, when Cyclone Arnab made landfall along the Andhra Pradesh–Yanam coast, Bharat’s strengthened disaster management framework effectively protected lives and property. According to official assessments of the response, accurate early weather forecasting, proactive mass evacuations, seamless coordination across government agencies, and the swift deployment of NDRF and SDRF personnel kept casualties and infrastructure damage to a minimum. The operation highlighted the country’s modern, self-reliant approach to handling severe natural calamities and safeguarding its citizens. This report highlights how Bharat has modernised its disaster management system since 2014 through policy reforms, resilient infrastructure, advanced technology, increased funding, and faster emergency responses to protect lives and property. Proactive Policy Approach: Bharat moved away from reactive relief toward advance preparedness through the 2016 National Disaster Management Plan (aligned with the UN Sendai Framework) and the Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda. Grassroots Volunteer Network: The Aapda Mitra scheme grew from 5,186 volunteers in 30 districts to a target of 1 lakh trained and insured community responders across 350 multi-hazard districts, alongside the Yuva Aapda Mitra initiative engaging NCC, NSS, and Bharat Scouts and Guides. Resilient Infrastructure: Bharat built cyclone shelters, evacuation roads, bridges, underground power cables, river embankments, Himalayan slope stabilization, and rockfall barriers to withstand severe weather events. Advanced Early-Warning Systems: Upgrades in weather tracking using Doppler radars, tsunami monitoring, storm-surge modelling, satellite drought assessments, and the Damini lightning-alert app, supported by the Rs 2,000 crore Mission Mausam for AI-based forecasting. Increased Funding and Rapid Action: For the 2021–26 period, allocations of Rs1.60 lakh crore for SDRF and SDMF, Rs54,770 crore for NDRF, and Rs13,693 crore for NDMF, while Inter-Ministerial Central Team (IMCT) deployment times dropped from 96 days to 8 days by 2025. Transforming Bharat’s Disaster Governance: A Shift Toward Proactive Resilience Since 2014, Bharat has fundamentally transformed its disaster governance framework, moving away from a reactive, post-disaster relief model toward a decisive, proactive strategy centred on early warnings, risk reduction, and minimising the loss of lives and property. Overcoming Past Fragmentation: Prior to 2014, despite the enactment of the Disaster Management Act of 2005, Bharat’s disaster response remained largely fragmented and reactive. Authorities often struggled with poor co-ordination, staffing shortages, and the lack of a unified operational strategy, which led to delayed responses during major crises. The Landmark National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP): A decisive turning point occurred in May 2016 with the launch of Bharat’s first comprehensive National Disaster Management Plan. Later updated in November 2019 to address climate change and localised risks, the NDMP established a clear, unified roadmap for the entire nation. Global Standards and “Build Back Better”: The NDMP aligned Bharat’s strategy with the four core priorities of the United Nations Sendai Framework (2015–2030): understanding disaster risks, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and enhancing response preparedness. It also embedded the principle of “Build Back Better” into recovery and reconstruction efforts. The Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda: Announced at the Asian Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in New Delhi in November 2016, the Prime Minister’s Ten-Point Agenda turned these broad goals into concrete action. Inclusive and Technology-Driven Development: This agenda mandated that all development sectors integrate disaster risk management into their projects. It placed a strong emphasis on safeguarding vulnerable households and small businesses, empowering women to take leadership roles in disaster management, and investing heavily in multi-hazard mapping, modern technology, and stronger institutions. Empowering Citizens on the Frontlines: Building a Self-Reliant Disaster Response Under the Modi government’s vision of Jan Bhagidari (people’s participation), Bharat has transformed disaster response from a purely government-led effort into a nationwide grassroots movement. By training ordinary citizens and youth as first responders, the nation is building a resilient, self-reliant society capable of protecting communities before formal relief forces even arrive. Massive Expansion of Aapda Mitra: Spearheaded by the Central Government through the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), the Aapda Mitra scheme trains local residents to act as immediate first responders. After a successful pilot between 2016 and 2018 that trained 5,186 volunteers across 30 flood-prone districts, the initiative was scaled up nationwide to certify and equip 1,00,000 community volunteers across 350 multi-hazard districts in every state and Union Territory. Hands-On Training by Elite Forces: Volunteers undergo an intensive five-day training program led by master trainers from the NDRF and SDRF. They learn life-saving skills including CPR, first aid, flood rescue, basic search and rescue, navigating collapsed structures, and safely evacuating vulnerable citizens. Comprehensive Gear and Insurance Protection: To ensure these grassroots heroes are well-protected, every trained volunteer receives an Emergency Responder Kit equipped with a safety helmet, life jacket, protective gear, LED torch, first-aid supplies, multi-tool knife, and emergency whistle. Additionally, the government provides each enrolled volunteer with three years of life and disability insurance coverage. Proven Impact on the Ground: Aapda Mitra volunteers have already proven their worth during major crises, including Cyclone Fani in Odisha, the Kerala floods, and the Wayanad landslide. Working shoulder-to-shoulder with local authorities, they played a crucial role in delivering early warnings, guiding evacuations, administering first aid, and distributing essential relief materials.
